titleStmt.title: An Efficient Utilization-based Test for Scheduling Hard Real-Time Sporadic DAG Task Systems on Multiprocessors

analytic.title: An Efficient Utilization-based Test for Scheduling Hard Real-Time Sporadic DAG Task Systems on Multiprocessors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The scheduling and schedulability analysis of real-time directed acyclic graph (DAG) task systems have received much recent attention. The DAG model can accurately represent intra-task parallelism and precedence constraints existing in many application domains. Existing techniques show that analyzing the DAG model is fundamentally more challenging compared to the ordinary sporadic task model, due to the complex intra-DAG precedence constraints which may cause rather pessimistic schedulability loss. However, such increased loss is counter-intuitive because the DAG structure shall better exploit the hardware parallelism provided by the multiprocessor platform. Our key observation is that the intra-DAG precedence constraints, if not carefully considered by the scheduling algorithm, may cause unpredictable execution behaviors of subtasks in a DAG and thus pessimistic analysis. In this paper, we present a set of novel scheduling and analysis techniques for better supporting hard real-time sporadic DAG tasks on multiprocessors, through smartly defining and analyzing the execution order of subtasks in each DAG. Combined with a new DAG-specific interval analysis framework, the proposed subtask ordering technique leads to a highly efficient utilization-based schedulability test. Importantly, the developed test becomes identical to the classical density test designed for the sporadic task model, if each DAG in the system has an out-degree of one (i.e., only containing a chain of subtasks). Experiments show the efficiency of the developed test, which improves schedulability upon existing utilization-based tests by over 60% on average and is often able to guarantee schedulability with little utilization loss.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In many real-time and embedded systems, applications are defined using processing graphs [1] to better exploit the parallel computing capability provided by the multicore platform. The scheduling and schedulability analysis of the real-time DAG (directed acyclic graph) model, which is defined to accurately capture such graph structure and intragraph precedence constraints, have received much recent attention [2]- [24]. Although the development of such works represents a major and promising step towards better supporting real-time DAG tasks on multiprocessors, they fundamentally suffer from intra-DAG precedence constraints and may exhibit pessimistic schedulability loss. By comparing such DAG-based tests with the tests developed for ordinary sporadic tasks, the DAG-induced schedulability loss becomes much more significant (also noted in [14], [16]). Nonetheless, we believe that such increased schedulability loss is counter-intuitive. If a DAG task system contains the same amount of workload as an ordinary sporadic task system, then the DAG task system shall be more easily schedulable because a DAG may better exploit the hardware parallelism provided by multiprocessors. Fig. 1 shows a simple example illustrating this intuition. As seen in Fig. 1(a), τ 3,1 misses its deadline if τ 3 is a sporadic task with an execution cost of three time units. Interestingly, if τ 3 were a DAG task (Fig. 1(c)) with the same total execution demand, then it would have becomes schedulable (Fig. 1(b)). This is because as a DAG task, τ 3 can benefit from the parallelism provided by the two-processor system.

This intuition motivates us to understand why the existing DAG-based schedulability analysis techniques (e.g., [14], [16]) indicate the opposite conclusion where DAG task systems are harder to schedule. We observe that a common consensus is that for ordinary sporadic tasks, a released job can start immediately given an idle processor; yet for DAG tasks, a released jobs from a subtask in a DAG can start only if all its predecessor jobs have completed, besides the premise of processor availability. This extra condition causes over pessimism in the analysis as the execution behaviors of subtasks in a DAG is unpredictable due to the precedence constraints among subtasks defined by the DAG structure. Existing scheduling algorithms such as global-earliest-deadline-rist (GEDF) are not smart enough to handle and further explore such complex DAG structures (also noted in [14]).

In this paper, we propose a set of novel scheduling methods and analysis techniques that enable the system to take the intuitive advantage of hardware parallelism for executing DAG tasks on multiprocessors. There are two major components in our proposed approach: a Lazy-Cpath policy and a new DAG-specific executing/non-executing interval-based analysis technique. The intuitive idea behind the Lazy-Cpath policy is to smartly define the execution order of ready jobs of subtasks belonging to the same DAG. By applying the Lazy-Cpath policy, intuitively, the resulting GEDF schedule would allow us to analyze the DAG tasks while mostly ignoring the complex intra-DAG precedence constraints. Combining the Lazy-Cpath policy with a novel executing/non-executing interval-based analysis technique, the resulting framework can more precisely characterize DAG-based workload distribution in the analysis window, which yields a rather efficient utilization-based test.

Overview of related work. Scheduling and schedulability analysis of hard real-time (HRT) DAG task systems have received much recent attention [6]- [20], [25], [26]. Capacity augmentation bounds have been derived under decomposition-based scheduling [7]- [11], where DAGs are transformed into sequential subtasks and scheduled under traditional schedulers [12]- [16]. Federated scheduling approaches have also been developed, which assign highutilization DAGs exclusively to dedicated processors and execute low-utilization DAGs as sequential sporadic tasks on the remaining processors [17]- [20], [25].

There exist two utilization-based schedulability tests [14], [16] for dealing with GEDF-scheduled HRT DAG task systems on multiprocessors. In [14], Li et al. proved that if an implicit-deadline DAG task system has a total utilization of at most M 4-2 M and each task's critical path (defined in Def. 2) length is no longer than 1 4-2 M of its deadline, it can be scheduled on a multiprocessor with M ≥ 2 processors under GEDF. In [16], Chen and Agrawal proved that if the total utilization of a DAG task system is at most
div.formula: M 1 1-Δmax +1-1 M
div.p: , where Δ max is the maximum critical path utilization among all DAGs in the system, then the implicit-deadline DAG task system can be feasibly scheduled under GEDF on M processors. Both tests show that the complex intra-DAG precedence constraints may cause rather pessimistic schedulability loss. Essentially, any DAG task system with a total utilization larger than M 3 will fail to pass the schedulability test provided in [14]; while any DAG task system with a total utilization larger than 2M 3 will fail to pass the test in [16].

Our contributions. In this paper, we develop an efficient utilization-based schedulability test for HRT sporadic DAG task systems scheduled on a multiprocessor with M identical cores under GEDF. Specifically, we show that any HRT DAG task system τ is schedulable under GEDF combined with the Lazy-Cpath policy which defines subtask ordering within each DAG, if for every task
div.formula: τ k ∈ τ , n i=1 η i ≤ M -(M -1) × σ k ,(1)
div.p: holds, where η i is defined in Eq. 6 and σ k denotes the total utilization of subtasks on the critical path of DAG τ k . This schedulability test can be viewed as the DAG version of the schedulability test derived for the ordinary sporadic task model given in [27], through replacing the constraint of σ k in Eq. 1 by τ k 's utilization. Intuitively, this test shows that the complex intra-DAG precedence constraints may not impose additional pessimism, as σ k does not depend on the specific precedence constraints seen in DAG τ k .

To derive this test, we develops a novel Lazy-Cpath policy that advises GEDF to execute the ready job of any subtask on the corresponding DAG's critical path as the last job among all ready jobs belonging to the same DAG at any time instant. Combining this subtask ordering method with a new DAG-specific executing/non-executing interval analysis technique, we are able to more precisely characterize the workload distribution in the analysis window of interest.

Experiments demonstrate that the above schedulability test is highly efficient, which dramatically improves schedulability compared to existing utilization-based tests by over 60% on average. Importantly, this test becomes identical to the classical density test 1 [28] designed for ordinary sporadic task systems, if each DAG task has an outdegree of 1 (i.e., only containing a chain of subtasks).

Another interesting observation on Eq. 1 is that a DAG task system may be schedulable even if its total utilization approaches M , if its maximum critical path utilization among all DAGs is not significantly large. The implication may be important for practical scenarios. Given the often large count of cores seen in many industrial systems (e.g., baseband processing), the DAG-based workloads often exhibit large outdegree, which implies that the critical path utilization σ k could be small compared to the corresponding DAG task utilization. This also complies with our fundamental intuition that DAGs shall benefit from running on multiprocessors, as the hardware parallelism could be well utilized by parallel DAG-based workloads.

div.head: System Model
div.p: We consider the problem of scheduling a set τ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } of n independent sporadic DAG tasks on M identical processors. Each task τ i is specified by a tuple
div.formula: (G i , d i , p i ), where G i = (V i , E i ) is a DAG
div.p: whose structure is defined by a set of subtasks V i and a set of edges E i connecting these subtasks, and d i and p i denote the relative deadline and period of DAG τ i , respectively. Let τ k i denote the k th subtask of τ i and τ k i,j denote the j th job of τ k i . A directed edge from subtask τ k i to τ h i implies that τ k i is a predecessor subtask of τ h i (also τ h i is a successor subtask of τ k i ). Thus, for any j, job τ k i,j is a predecessor job of τ h i,j . Any job of any subtask is ready to start executing if all of its predecessor jobs have completed.

Each sporadic DAG task τ i generates an infinite sequence of dag-jobs, with arrival times of successive jobs separated by at least p i time units. Clearly, each dag-job released by τ i is composed by |V i | jobs belonging to the |V i | subtasks. Thus, the j th jobs of all subtasks in τ i share a same release time denoted by r i,j and a same absolute deadline denoted by d i,j = r i,j + d i . Each subtask has a worst case execution time e k i . Our DAG model allows multiple source subtasks (i.e., those with no predecessor subtask) and sink subtask (i.e., with no successor subtask) are allowed in our general DAG model. In this paper, we focus our attention on implicit-deadline DAG task systems, where d i = p i holds for all DAG tasks.
div.formula: Definition 1. (Critical Path of a DAG) A chain in DAG τ i is a sequence of subtasks τ x1 i , τ x2 i , . . . , τ xz i ∈ V i such that (τ xu i , τ xu+1 i ) is an edge in G i , 1 ≤ u < z -1.
div.p: The length of this chain is defined to be the sum of the execution times of all the subtasks on the chain:
div.formula: z u=1 e xu i .
div.p: We denote by Cpath i = {τ x1 i , τ x2 i , . . . , τ x k i } the longest chain, named tje critical path of DAG τ i . Let len(Cpath i ) denote the length of Cpath i . Each DAG has only one critica path. Note that there may exist multiple paths with the same maximum length among all paths in a DAG task. In such cases, we arbitrarily select one from them as the only critical path of this DAG. 2 Definition 2. (cp-utilization) For each DAG τ i , we define σ i = len(Cpath i )/p i as the cp-utilization of τ i , which represents the total utilization of subtasks on the critical path of τ i .
We now define several additional terminologies for the DAG task model:
div.formula: • We denote by C i = |Vi| v=1 e v
div.p: i the total execution time of each DAG τ i .
For each DAG τ i we define a utilization u i = C i /p i . The total utilization of the DAG task system is
div.formula: U sum = n i=1 u i .
div.p: • For a sporadic DAG task system τ , we define its maximum cp-utilization σ max (τ ) to be the largest cp-utilization of any task in τ : σ max (τ ) = max τi∈τ σ i . We require len(Cpath i ) ≤ p i , and U sum ≤ M ; otherwise, deadlines will be missed. Successive dag-jobs released by the same DAG are required to execute in sequence. We study the DAG task system under preemptive GEDF scheduling: dag-jobs with earlier deadlines are assigned higher priorities. Note that all jobs released by the subtasks in a DAG inherit the same priority assigned to the corresponding dag-job. We assume that ties are broken by task ID (lower IDs are favored). Throughout the paper, we assume that time is integral. Thus, a job that executes at time instant t executes during the entire time interval [t, t + 1).

div.head: Subtask Ordering: The Lazy-Cpath Policy
div.p: Due to intra-DAG precedence constraints, analyzing the schedulability of DAG task systems on a multiprocessor could be more challenging compared to the case of ordinary sporadic tasks. Precedence constraints among subtasks in a DAG make it hard to precisely analyze the subtasks' execution behavior and bound the interference workload upon certain analyzed jobs, as shown in several recent works [13]- [16]. For instance, a recent work [14] demonstrated this challenge by assuming worst-case interference scenarios due to precedence constraints and developing a utilization-based schedulability test for a sporadic DAG task system. The following quote can be found in the abstract of [14]:
"For the proposed capacity augmentation bound of 4-2 M for implicit deadline tasks under GEDF, we prove that if a task set has a total utilization of at most M

div.head: M
div.p: and each task's critical path length is no more than

of its deadline, it can be scheduled on a machine with M processors under GEDF. For the standard resource augmentation bound of 2 -1 M for arbitrary deadline tasks under GEDF, we prove that if an ideal optimal scheduler can schedule a task set on M unitspeed processors, then GEDF can schedule the same task set on M processors of speed 2 -1 M . However, this bound does not lead to a schedulability test since the ideal optimal scheduler is only hypothetical and is not known."

When tasks are scheduled on a multiprocessor platform (M ≥ 2), the above schedulability test [14] essentially requires that the total system utilization is no greater than M 3 and each task's critical path length is no more than 1 3 of its deadline. Such constraints are rather pessimistic.

As quoted above, designing a good scheduler is critical to develop a corresponding efficient schedulability test. Our goal is thus to design a smarter runtime scheduler that efficiently supports DAG task scheduling on multiprocessors. In the rest of this section, we propose a Lazy-Cpath policy to precisely define the execution order of subtasks in a DAG. By combing the Lazy-Cpath policy with GEDF, the resulting scheduler yields several important properties about and τ 4 1,1 due to the Lazy-Cpath policy.
the execution behavior of the DAG tasks, which enable us to develop significantly improved schedulability tests.

div.head: The Lazy-Cpath Policy
div.p: We now formally define the Lazy-Cpath Policy and derive its beneficial properties that enable us to develop an efficient schedulability test. The Lazy-Cpath policy: Under the Lazy-Cpath policy, at any time instance, ready jobs of subtasks on a DAG's critical path has the lowest priority among all ready jobs of subtasks belonging to the same DAG. Note that for any DAG, at most one subtask on its critical path could have a ready job, because subtasks on any DAG's critical path form a single chain of subtasks whose released jobs must be executed sequentially. Thus, under the Lazy-Cpath policy, GEDF works as follows: at each time instant, the scheduler first tries to schedule as many ready jobs with the earliest deadlines; if the number of such ready jobs is larger than M , then GEDF first schedules ready jobs of subtasks that are not on the critical path of the corresponding DAG. Let CP-GEDF denote the scheduling strategy after applying the Lazy-Cpath policy to GEDF.

According to the above definition, the Lazy-Cpath policy does not define specific execution order among jobs of subtasks that are not on the critical path. Rather, it forces the ready jobs of subtasks on the critical path of each DAG to have the lowest priority among all ready jobs belonging to that DAG. Thus, under the Lazy-Cpath policy, jobs of subtasks on the critical path of any DAG are executed as the last among all ready jobs of that DAG. Also note that for each dag-job, any executing jobs of subtasks on the DAG's critical path may be preempted by newly released (and ready) jobs of subtasks which are not on the DAG's critical path.

Example 2. Fig. 3 shows that an example DAG τ 1 scheduled on 2 processors under CP-GEDF. The DAG structure is shown in Fig. 3(a), where vertices are labeled with the corresponding execution times. The critical path of τ 1 is τ 1 1 ⇒ τ 5 1 ⇒ τ 6 1 . Fig. 3(b) shows the schedule for the first dag-job of τ 1 . As seen in the figure, τ 5 1,1 starts executing at time instant 10. But according to the Lazy-Cpath policy, it gets preempted by τ 3 1,1 and τ 4 1,1 at time instant 15.

div.head: Beneficial Properties of the Lazy-Cpath policy
div.p: We now derive beneficial properties of the CP-GEDF schedule. Let τ x1 i,j , τ x2 i,j , . . . , τ x k i,j denote the jobs of subtasks on the critical path for any dag-job τ i,j . Let t xu i,j denote the time instant when τ xu i,j starts executing. Lemma 1. If we schedule a set τ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } of n independent sporadic DAG tasks on M identical processors under CP-GEDF, any job τ
belonging to the critical path of dag-job τ i,j becomes ready when its predecessor job τ xu i,j belonging to the critical path completes.

Proof. Let S denote the CP-GEDF schedule and f xu i,j denote the completion time of job τ xu i,j . To prove this lemma, it suffices to prove that the job τ xu i,j belonging to the critical path is the last completed job among all predecessor jobs of τ xu+1 i,j . We prove this new proof obligation by contradiction. Assume that τ xu+1 i,j has another predecessor job τ y1 i,j which completes later than τ xu i,j . Let f y1 i,j denote the completion time of τ y1 i,j . Since under GEDF, dag-jobs released by different DAG tasks have distinct priorities and all jobs belonging to a dagjob inherit the same priority of the dag-job, the relative execution ordering of all jobs belonging to dag-job τ i,j including τ xu i,j and τ y1 i,j does not depend on other dag-jobs, but solely depends on the DAG structure of τ i and the Lazy-Cpath policy.
We analyze the interval
div.formula: [r i,j , f y1 i,j ) by dividing it into w ≥ 1 time intervals, denoted by [f y2 i,j , f y1 i,j ), [f y3 i,j , f y2 i,j ), . . . , [r i,j , f yw i,j
div.p: ), ordered from right to left with respect to time, as illustrated in Fig. 4. We identify these time intervals by moving from right to left with respect to time in the schedule S considering jobs belonging to the dag-job τ i,j .

We identify this interval set by finding a path in τ i starting from a source subtask and ending at the subtask τ y1 i . Moving from the time instant f y1 i,j to the left in S, let f y2 i,j denote the latest completion time among τ y1 i,j 's predecessor jobs. Note that τ y1 i,j becomes ready at f y2 i,j . We thus identify the first interval[f y2 i,j , f y1 i,j ) in this set. Moving from f y2 i,j to the left in S, we apply this same process to identify the remaining intervals in this set, until we find the source subtask τ yw i for this path, which is ready at the release time of the corresponding dag-job τ i,j at r i,j and completes at f yw i,j . Note that this path always exists because τ y1 i,j exists. We now show a contradiction that there exists another path consisting of τ yw i , . . . , τ y1 i , τ
div.formula: xu+1 i , . . . , τ x k i that is longer than the critical path of τ i . For each time interval [f yq+1 i,j , f yq i,j ) (2 ≤ q ≤ w -1)
div.p: , we know that τ yq i,j is ready at the beginning of this interval f yq+1 i,j according to the definition of the interval. Thus, each interval
div.formula: [f yq+1 i,j , f yq i,j ) (includ- ing [r i,j , f yw i,j
div.p: )) only consists of two kinds of subintervals: (i) subintervals during which τ yq i,j executes continuously, and (ii) subintervals during which τ yq i,j are not executing (i.e., being preempted by jobs belonging to other dag-jobs with higher priorities than τ i,j or being delayed by jobs belonging to the same dag-job). During the first kind of subintervals, jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i may execute; but during the second kind of subintervals, jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i do not execute due to the Lazy-Cpath policy, for otherwise τ yq i,j should have been executing during such subintervals. Thus, during each
div.formula: [f yq+1 i,j , f yq i,j ) ((2 ≤ q ≤ w -1)
div.p: ), the workload executed due to τ yq i,j is at least the workload due to jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i . Moreover, within the last interval [f y2 i,j , f y1 i,j ), since τ y1 i,j completes later than τ xu i,j , we know that the workload executed due to τ y1 i,j must be strictly greater than the workload due to jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i . Therefore, the total workload executed within [r i,j , f y1 i,j ) due to the subtask set {τ yw i , . . . , τ y2 i , τ y1 i } must be strictly greater than the total workload due to the subset of subtasks on the critical path of τ i (this subset including subtasks on the partial critical path starting from the source subtask on the critical path and ending at τ xu i ). Clearly, we have identified another path in τ i , composed by
div.formula: τ yw i ⇒ τ yw-1 i ⇒ • • • ⇒ τ y2 i ⇒ τ y1 i ⇒ τ xu+1 i ⇒ Γ,
div.p: where Γ represents the remaining subtasks following τ xu+1 i on the critical path of τ i . And this path is longer than the critical path of τ i . A contradiction is reached.

Lemma 2. If we schedule a set τ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } of n independent sporadic DAG tasks on M identical processors under CP-GEDF, a dag-job τ i,j of τ i completes its execution when the job τ x k i,j of the last subtask τ x k i on the critical path complete its execution.

Proof. This lemma can be proved in the same manner as lemma 1, by reaching a contradiction where an identified path in τ i is longer than the critical path of τ i . For completeness, we put the detailed proof in the appendix.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: We now present our schedulability analysis for DAG task systems scheduled under CP-GEDF. Our approach is fundamentally based on the window-based reasoning framework which was first proposed by Baker [27] and has been used extensively to analyze the ordinary sporadic task model [29]- [31]. Due to the complex DAG structure and intra-DAG precedence constraints, the original windowbased reasoning could not precisely characterize the workload distribution in an analysis window. We first enhance this framework by developing a novel executing/non-executing critical path interval analysis technique.

div.head: Executing/Non-Executing Intervals
div.p: We first present the formal definition of an executing/non-executing critical path interval.

div.head: Definition 3. (Executing/non-executing critical path interval
div.formula: ) A time interval [t 1 , t 2
div.p: ) is an executing critical path interval for τ i if the following three conditions hold: (i) a DAG job τ i,j of τ i is released at or before t 1 ; (ii) τ i,j completes its execution no earlier than t 2 ; (iii) jobs of subtasks on τ i 's critical path are executing continuously throughout this interval. Otherwise, if conditions (i) and (ii) hold, but no job of any subtask on τ i 's critical path executes at any time instant within [t 1 , t 2 ), then [t 1 , t 2 ) is a non-executing critical path interval for τ i .

div.head: Definition 4. (Busy interval) a time instant t is a busy instant if all M processors execute jobs at t. A time interval
div.formula: [t 1 , t 2 ) is busy if every time instant t in [t 1 , t 2 ) is busy.
div.p: Example 3. Fig. 5 shows that two DAG tasks are scheduled on two processors under CP-GEDF. The DAG structures for τ 1 and τ 2 are shown in Fig. 5(a) and Fig. 5(b), where the execution cost for each subtask is 10 time units. Fig. 5(c) shows the schedule for the first dag-jobs of τ 1 and τ 2 . Since the periods of τ 1 and τ 2 are 40 time units and 50 time units, respectively, and both τ 1 and τ 2 release the first dag-jobs at time 0, jobs belonging to the first dag-job of τ 1 have higher priorities than those of τ 2 . According to the DAG structure, the critical path of τ 2 is τ 1 2 ⇒ τ 3 2 ⇒ τ 4 2 . As seen in the Fig. 5(c),τ 1 2,1 starts executing at time 0, but τ 3 2,1 is preempted during [10,30) according to GEDF-CP. In this example, [0, 10) and [30,50) are executing critical path intervals for τ 2 , and [10,30) is a non-executing critical path interval for τ 2 . [0, 30) is clearly a busy interval.

div.head: Lemma 3. In the CP-GEDF schedule for a DAG task system
div.formula: τ , if [t 1 , t 2 ) is a non-executing critical path interval for τ i , then [t 1 , t 2 ) is a busy interval.
div.p: Proof. Let τ i,j denote the dag-job that is released before t 1 and does not complete before t 2 . We prove this lemma by contradiction. Suppose [t 1 , t 2 ) is a non-executing critical path interval for τ i , and [t 1 , t 2 ) is not a busy interval. By Def. 4, at least one processor is idle during [t 1 , t 2 ). By Lemma 2, some jobs of subtasks on τ i 's critical path have not completed before t 2 . Let β denote the set of such jobs. Note that β must exist because at least the job of the last subtask on τ i 's critical path has not completed before t 2 . According to Lemma 1, there must be a job in β , denoted by J, that is ready at t 1 . Thus, J must be executing on the idle processor during [t 1 , t 2 ). However, by Def. 3, no job of any subtask on τ i 's critical path shall execute at any time instant within [t 1 , t 2 ). A contradiction is thus reached.

div.head: A Necessary Condition for Deadline Misses
div.p: We focus on analyzing what happens when a deadline is missed given any DAG task system τ scheduled under CP-GEDF on M identical processors. Let t d denote the first time instant in any such schedule S at which a deadline is missed. Let dag-job τ h,l be the one that misses its deadline d h,l at t d , which is released by task τ h at r h,l . Note that dagjobs with deadlines later than t d do not affect the scheduling of dag-jobs with deadlines no later than t d . Thus, we remove every dag-job with a deadline later than t d from S. The following lower bound on the average workload of a problem window can be observed in the schedule S, which is a necessary condition for τ h,l to miss its deadline.

div.head: Lemma 4. Since τ h,l misses its deadline at t d , the sum of the lengths of all non-executing critical path intervals for
div.formula: τ h within [r h,l , t d ) must exceed p h -len(Cpath h ).
div.p: Proof. According to lemma 2, a dag-job completes when the job of the last subtask on its critical path completes. Since τ h,l has not completed by t d , the job of the last subtask on τ h 's critical path has not completed by t d . We can divide [r h,l , t d ) into subintervals including either executing or non-executing critical path intervals for τ h by Def. 3. Since the jobs of subtasks on the critical path must execute sequentially, this lemma immediately follows.

div.head: Window-based Analysis
div.p: We now present a window-based analysis for upperbounding the workload W within the problem window, which allows us to derive a test using Lemma 5.

For any DAG τ i that may execute in a problem window of interest, we divide this window into three sub-windows including the head, the body, and the tail sub-window. The workload contributed by τ i in this window, denoted by W i , is the sum of the workload contributed by τ i within these three sub-windows. We seek to obtain a total upper bound on W i by seperately upper-bounding the workload contribution of τ i in each sub-window. This concept is illustrated in Fig. 7. The head of a window [t d -Δ, t d ) is defined to be interval [t d -Δ, t d -Δ + min{Δ, p i -λ}), if there exists a dag-job of DAG task τ i that is released at time t = t d -Δ-λ and 0 < λ < p i . Such a dag-job is called the carry-in dag-job of τ i w.r.t. this problem window (formally defined in Def. 10). Note that if such a carry-in dag-job of τ i does not exist, τ i does not contribute any workload within the head sub-window. Besides the head sub-window, the tail sub-window exists if τ i releases a dag-job before t d which has a deadline later than t d . The remaining interval within [t d -Δ, t d ) is defined to be the body sub-window.

Based on the above definition, it is straightforward to upper bound the workload contributed by τ i during the body sub-window through upper-bounding the number of dagjobs released by τ i in the body sub-window. Moreover, τ i does not contribute any workload during the tail sub-window under CP-GEDF, since we already removed dag-jobs with deadlines later than t d from S. The challenge mainly lies in upper-bounding the workload contributed by τ i within the head sub-window. In the rest of this section, we first derive a workload upper bound within the head sub-window in Lemmas 7 and 8, and then derive the overall workload W i within the entire problem window in Lemma 10.

div.head: A Utilization-based Schedulability Test
div.p: We now use Lemma 10 combined with Lemma 5, which is the necessary condition for deadline misses given in Sec. 4.2, to derive a utilization-based schedulability test.
div.formula: Theorem 1. A set τ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } of n independent spo- radic DAG tasks is schedulable on M identical processors under CP-GEDF, if, for every task τ k , n i=1 η i ≤ M -(M -1) × σ k . (7

div.head: Experiments
div.p: We have conducted extensive sets of experiments using randomly-generated DAG task sets to evaluate the applica- Figure 9: Schedulability results. In all graphs, the x-axis represents the task set utilization cap and the y-axis represents the fraction of generated task sets that were schedulable. In the first (respectively, second) rows of graphs, M = 8 (respectively, M = 16) is assumed. In the first (respectively, second and third) column of graphs, light (respectively, medium and heavy) pertask utilizations are assumed. Each graph gives seven curves: two curves per tested approach for DAG task sets for the cases of short and long critical path, respectively, and one additional curve of the density test for ordinary sporadic task sets. As seen at the top of the figure, the label "CP-GEDF-s(l)" indicates the approach of our schedulability test given in Theorem 1 assuming short (long) critical path. Similarly, "SU-s(l)" and "CAB-s(l)" labels denote the utilization-based schedulability tests given in [16] and [14]; "MC-s(l)" label denotes schedulability test given in [32] with a simplified criticality setting; "CB" label denotes the utilization bound given in [17]. bility of Theorem 1. We compare our test denoted "CP-GEDF" with two existing utilization-based schedulability tests: one denoted by "CAB" given by Corollary 6 in [14], and the second one denoted by "SU" given by Corollary 2 in [16]. As the capacity augmentation bound of 2.73 given in [17] can be transferred to a utilization bound of M/2.73, we improve the evaluation by adding a comparison with it, which is denoted by "CB". [32] defined a meta-heuristic to schedule multiprocessor systems composed of multiperiodic Mixed-Criticality DAG tasks. We also expand the evaluation by adding a comparison considering the test given in [32] with a simplified criticality setting, which is denoted by "MC".

Experimental setup: We adopted the popular Erdos-Renyi method [33] to generate the structure of DAGs in our experiments, which has also been used in previous works such as [14]. Task periods were uniformly distributed over [50ms, 200ms]. Task utilizations were distributed differently for each experiment using three uniform distributions. The ranges for the uniform distributions were [0.005, 0.5] (light), [0.5, 1] (medium), and [1, 1.5] (heavy). Each DAG's execution time was calculated from the corresponding period and utilization values. The cp-utilization of each DAG was generated using two uniform distributions: [0.1×u i , 0.3×u i ] (critical paths are relatively short), and [0.3 × u i , 0.5 × u i ] (critical paths are relatively long). We varied the total system utilization U sum within {0.1, 0.2, . . . , M}. For each combination of per-DAG task utilization, cp-utilization, and U sum , 1,000 task sets were generated for systems with 8 or 16 processors. Each such task set was generated by creating tasks until total utilization exceeding the corresponding utilization cap, and by then increasing the last task's period so that the total utilization equals the utilization cap. For each generated set, HRT schedulability was checked under CP-GEDF, CAB, SU and MC.

Another interesting comparison examined in our experiments is to verify whether our derived test takes advantage of the intra-DAG parallelism. That is, whether does the intra-DAG parallelism help a DAG task system easier to be schedulable on a multiprocessor compared to ordinary sporadic task systems. For this evaluation, for each generated DAG set, we generate a corresponding sporadic task set where each sporadic task τ i has the same utilization as the utilization of each DAG task τ i (the total utilization of subtasks of the DAG). We check the schedulability of each such generated sporadic task set by the classic density test [28], denoted as "U-ordinary". Note that if any generated DAG task in an experiment set has a utilization greater than one, then we choose not to compare CP-GEDF with U-ordinary for that experiment set. Experimental results: The experimental schedulability results are shown in Fig. 9 (the organization of each sub-figure is described in the figure's caption). Each curve represents the fraction of the generated task sets successfully scheduled by the corresponding approach, as a function of the total system utilization. As seen in the figure, under all tested scenarios, CP-GEDF improves upon MC, SU, CAB and CB by a notable margin. For example, in Fig. 9(b), when DAGs' critical paths are short and per-task utilization is medium, CP-GEDF-s can achieve 100% schedulability when U sum is not exceeding 6 while MC, SU, CB and CAB tests fail to do so when U sum merely exceeds 3.75, 3.25 2.75 and 1.25, respectively. 3 Note that in Fig. 9(c) and Fig. 9(f), when tasks' critical paths are long and per-task utilization is heavy, no task set can pass the CAB test.

The experimental results also verify that our schedulability test explores the intuition where the DAG task model may better benefit from the multiprocessor parallelism compared to the sporadic task model. As seen in Fig. 9(a), Fig. 9(b), Fig. 9(d) and Fig. 9(e), CP-GEDF improves upon U-ordinary by rather large margins. This is because with the same per-task utilization, the cp-utilization for each DAG task is smaller than the task utilization for each ordinary sporadic task. According to our test and the classical density test, it is easier for the DAG task set to pass the schedulability test (Theorem 1).

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we present a set of novel scheduling and analysis techniques for better supporting hard real-time sporadic DAG tasks on multiprocessors, through smartly defining and analyzing the execution order of subtasks in each DAG. As demonstrated by experimental results, our proposed test significantly improves upon existing utilizationbased tests with respect to schedulability, and is often able to guarantee schedulability with little or no utilization loss.

Proof. Let S denote the CP-GEDF schedule and f xu i,j denote the completion time of job τ xu i,j . To prove this lemma, it suffices to prove that the job τ x k i,j , which is the last job of the critical path, is the last completed job among all jobs belonging to dag-job τ i,j . We prove this new proof obligation by contradiction. Assume that another job τ y0 i,j which completes later than τ x k i,j . Since under GEDF, dag-jobs released by different DAG tasks have distinct priorities and all jobs belonging to a dagjob inherit the same priority of the dag-job, the relative execution ordering of all jobs belonging to dag-job τ i,j 3. Let CP-GEDF-s (CP-GEDF-l) denote the case with short (long) critical paths. including τ xu i,j and τ y0 i,j does not depend on other dag-jobs, but solely depends on the DAG structure of τ i and the Lazy-Cpath policy.

We analyze the interval [r i,j , f y0 i,j ) by dividing it into w ≥ 1 time intervals, denoted by [f y1 i,j , f y0 i,j ), [f y2 i,j , f y1 i,j ), . . . , [r i,j , f yw i,j ), ordered from right to left with respect to time. We identify these time intervals by moving from right to left with respect to time in the schedule S considering jobs belonging to the dag-job τ i,j .

We identify this interval set by finding a path in τ i starting from a source subtask and ending at the subtask τ y0 i . Moving from the time instant f y0 i,j to the left in S, let f y1 i,j denote the latest completion time among τ y0 i,j 's predecessor jobs. Note that τ y0 i,j becomes ready at f y1 i,j . We thus identify the first interval[f y1 i,j , f y0 i,j ) in this set. Moving from f y1 i,j to the left in S, we apply this same process to identify the remaining intervals in this set, until we find the source subtask τ yw i for this path, which is ready at the release time of the corresponding dag-job τ i,j at r i,j and completes at f yw i,j . Note that this path always exists because τ y0 i,j exists. We now show a contradiction that there exists another path consisting of τ yw i , . . . , τ y2 i , τ y1 i , τ y0 i that is longer than the critical path of τ i . For each time interval [f yq+1 i,j , f yq i,j ) (1 ≤ q ≤ w -1), we know that τ yq i,j is ready at the beginning of this interval f yq+1 i,j according to the definition of the interval. Thus, each interval
div.formula: [f yq+1 i,j , f yq i,j ) (including [r i,j , f yw i,j
div.p: )) only consists of two kinds of subintervals: (i) subintervals during which τ yq i,j executes continuously, and (ii) subintervals during which τ yq i,j are not executing (i.e., being preempted by jobs belonging to other dag-jobs with higher priorities than τ i,j or being delayed by jobs belonging to the same dag-job). During the first kind of subintervals, jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i may execute; but during the second kind of subintervals, jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i do not execute due to the Lazy-Cpath policy, for otherwise τ yq i,j should have been executing during such subintervals. Thus, during each [f yq+1 i,j , f yq i,j ), the workload executed due to τ yq i,j is at least the workload due to jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i . Moreover, within the last interval [f y1 i,j , f y0 i,j ), since τ y0 i,j completes later than τ x k i,j , we know that the workload executed due to τ y0 i,j must be strictly greater than the workload due to jobs from the subtasks on the critical path of τ i . Therefore, the total workload executed within [r i,j , f y0 i,j ) due to the subtask set {τ yw i , . . . , τ y1 i , τ y0 i } must be strictly greater than the total workload due to the subset of subtasks on the critical path of τ i .
Clearly, we have identified another path in τ i and this path is longer than the critical path of τ i . A contradiction is reached.

Proof. The workload contributed by τ i in [t d -Δ, t d ), denoted by W i , is the sum of the workload contributed by τ i within three sub-windows. Our method is to identify a worst-case situation, where W i achieves the largest possible value for τ i in [t d -Δ, t d ). Note that under CP-GEDF, the contribution of any dag-job released by τ i in the tail subwindow is zero w.r.t. W i as such dag-jobs have deadlines later than t d . We will first consider the case where Δ ≥ p i , and then the other case where Δ < p i . Case 1: Δ ≥ p i . As illustrated in Fig. 10, it is evident that the maximum contribution due to τ i in the body sub-window is achieved when the dag-jobs within the body sub-window are released periodically and the last such dag-job has the deadline at t d . Thus, the number of completed dag-jobs of τ i in the body sub-window is clearly upper-bounded by Δ pi . According to Lemma 8, the upper bound of the carryin workload of τ i is C i -Δ × λ which is a non-increasing function of λ. Therefore, the carry-in workload is maximized when λ is minimized. However, this causes the number of released dag-jobs of τ i to be reduced by one within the body sub-window. Because [t d -Δ, t d ) includes the head sub-window and the body sub-window, when we decrease λ, the length of the head sub-window increases and the length of body sub-window decreases.
